evidence_quotes.quote: This study examines women's participation in governance of rural water
Five communities (Ga, Dorimon, Zanko, Vieri, and Naaha) were selected for the study
The study used a single-case study research design.
The study revealed that maintenance payments are not made on a regular basis.
both male and female members of the WSMTs were allowed to participate and share

country.comment: Conducted in five rural communities (Ga, Dorimon, Zanko, Vieri, and Naaha) in the Wa West District, Upper West Region, Ghana.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Abstract; PDF p. 7, Section 3.1

effect_estimate.comment: Primary qualitative study reporting thematic findings from 5 FGDs and field observations; no statistical point estimates or inferential tests are reported.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Across five rural communities in Ghana's Wa West District, women and men on Water and Sanitation Management Teams (WSMTs) participate without restriction and formulate borehole operation and maintenance rules by consensus without voting, with women actively initiating rules, conducting routine functionality checks, reporting faults, and contributing event-driven repair fees in some communities (GH₵ 2 for women in Naaha and Ga; GH₵ 1–7 for men across most communities). Communities enacted local rules prohibiting children from operating handpumps, locking boreholes overnight (7:00–7:30 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. in Ga) or when early signs of malfunction appear, banning urination/defecation near boreholes (within 200 m in Zanko) and waste dumping (enforced in Vieri with a GH₵ 100 fine and solo cleaning, and temporary water-fetching bans for repeat violators in Dorimon, Vieri, and Ga), barring borehole water use for brick molding, and banning metal cooking pots in Naaha; however, field observations documented weak enforcement, with children continuing to operate boreholes despite formal bans.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 10–17, Sections 5.1–5.3, Fig. 2, and Table 2

mechanism_certainty.comment: Qualitative case study (design ceiling = 2 per CODEBOOK.md §9) that directly documents and observes community governance mechanisms—consensus rule-making, women's participation in WSMTs, event-driven repair fee collection, overnight borehole locking, fines/fetching bans, and enforcement gaps observed at borehole sites—operating on rural water access and functionality.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 10–17, Sections 5.1–5.3, Fig. 2, and Table 2

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines women's and men's deliberative participation in WSMT rule-making and monitoring (participation), event-driven borehole repair contributions calibrated to community members' capacity to pay (fees), and local rule enforcement via monetary fines, mandatory cleaning, overnight locking, and temporary water-fetching bans alongside observed enforcement gaps (sanction).
mechanism_flags.value: BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, fees, participation, sanction

outcome_flags.comment: Examines community access to borehole drinking water including restrictions during locked hours and bans for repeat violators (water_access), borehole breakdown prevention and timely repair (service_reliability), restricted operating hours via overnight locking from 7:00–7:30 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. and early-malfunction closures (service_continuity), hygiene buffers around boreholes to prevent water contamination (service_quality), and setting event-driven repair contributions based on community members' financial strength to avoid burdensome regular fees (affordability).

publication_year.comment: Published in 2025 in Discover Water (volume 5, article 55; received 31 March 2025, accepted 30 June 2025).
publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, article header and copyright line; PDF p. 21, publication history

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary qualitative study using purposive sampling, 5 focus group discussions, field observations, and manual inductive thematic analysis; appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist.

sample_size.comment: Purposive sample of 37 active WSMT members (18 male, 19 female) across 5 rural communities (Ga: 8, Dorimon: 7, Zanko: 8, Vieri: 7, Naaha: 7), with 1 focus group discussion per community (5 FGDs total) plus direct field observations.
sample_size.value: 37 WSMT members (18 male, 19 female) across 5 focus group discussions in 5 rural communities
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 9, Sections 4.1–4.2; PDF p. 10, Table 1

study_design.comment: Authors describe a qualitative phenomenological approach within a single-case study design (Wa West District), operationalized via 5 community FGDs using structured interview guides, field observations with photographic documentation, and manual inductive thematic analysis.
study_design.value: Qualitative phenomenological single-case study (focus group discussions, field observations, and inductive thematic analysis)
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 8–10, Sections 4, 4.1, and 4.2
